stops.name: Santiago de Chile, Calle Santo Domingo, the birth
stops.campa: On the tenth of September, in a house on Calle Santo Domingo, Miguel Joaquín Diego del Carmen Serrano Fernández is born into an old Chilean family, criollo and Basque and Castilian, that came to the kingdom with the conquest. Beyond the flat roofs of the capital the Andes stand white and enormous, the eastern wall of the world. The child is set down at the foot of the cordillera that will be his temple and his cosmology to the end. He will call his life a single ascent toward the Mountain, and here, in the shadow of the snow, the ascent begins.

stops.name: Valle del Claro, the seventeenth-century mansion
stops.campa: His mother Berta dies when he is five; three years on his father Diego follows her into the ground. Orphaned, Miguel and his brothers and sister pass into the keeping of the grandmother, Fresia Manterola de Serrano, between a Santiago townhouse and a seventeenth-century casona in the Valle del Claro. In the country house the boy walks vineyards and old galleries where the dead of the family seem to linger; the early loss opens in him the wound he will spend his life sealing: the search for what does not die, for the Beloved beyond death, for A-Mor.

stops.name: Internado Nacional Barros Arana, Santiago
stops.campa: From 1929 he boards at the Internado Nacional Barros Arana, a school of Prussian severity and cold dormitories. Here the boy who has lost his parents finds a second family in books and in a circle of young writers; here too, he will say, the Germanophile spark is struck that will never leave him. He reads voraciously, the Romantics, Nietzsche, the sagas of the North, and begins to dream of a heroic order beyond the grey Republic, of initiation, of a hidden brotherhood into which a man might be reborn.

stops.name: Santiago, the Generation of '38 and the poet Huidobro
stops.campa: In the cafés of Calle San Diego and Avenida Matta the youth of the Generation of '38 gather: Héctor Barreto, Teófilo Cid, the strange Juan Emar. Serrano moves among them as poet, kin to the great creacionista Vicente Huidobro, who is his uncle and whose praise he covets. At twenty-one he assembles an anthology of the Chilean realist tale, a milestone of the national letters. He is a poet first; a poet, the exiled Armando Uribe will call him at the last, 'the truest poet.' The avant-garde and the mountain-worship live in him together.

stops.name: Santiago, the Seguro Obrero massacre, Calle Morandé
stops.campa: On the fifth of September the young Chilean National Socialists rise, are cornered in the Caja del Seguro Obrero on Calle Morandé, surrender, and are shot down almost to a man. The massacre scars Serrano forever; the sacrificed youths become, in his memory, martyrs of a doomed heroism. He turns from the left toward which Barreto's death had pushed him, seeks out the movement's leaders, and thereafter reads politics as sacred war. The blood on Morandé is, for him, an initiation into loss and defeated nobility: a wound he will never let close.

stops.name: Santiago, the review La Nueva Edad
stops.campa: From July of 1941 Serrano launches his own fortnightly, La Nueva Edad, 'The New Age,' a review of politics and letters through which he casts Chile's neutrality against the tide of the war. Here, in the printed word, he first sets down the mythic frame that will govern his whole cosmos: a New Age dawning, a hidden order of initiates, a war of the visible against the invisible. His uncle Huidobro praises his prose. The poet of the mountain has become the herald of a myth he will spend seven decades enlarging.

stops.name: The Andes above Santiago, the mountain as temple
stops.campa: In the great climbs of his youth Serrano goes up into the cordillera as into a cathedral. The Andes are for him no mere geology but the visible spine of the sacred, a temple of stone and light where the air thins and the self burns away. On the high glaciers he feels the presence he will chase across the world: the Mountain that is also the Self, the pole of the spirit. Mountaineering, for him, is prayer; the summit is a threshold. Every later journey, to the ice and to the Himalaya, is a repetition of this first ascent.

stops.name: Valparaíso, embarkation for the Antarctic
stops.campa: Serrano ships out from the Chilean coast with the Second Chilean Antarctic Expedition, carried south as a reporter for Zig-Zag and El Mercurio, his despatches read the length of the Republic. He goes, he will confess only years later, with a secret aim: to draw near the polar entrances of the legend, the openings at the ends of the earth into the Inner World. The Southern Ocean opens grey and vast before the bow. He is sailing not merely toward Antarctica but toward the mystery that will hold his cosmology to the last day of his life.

stops.name: Base Soberanía, Greenwich Island, South Shetlands
stops.campa: The expedition raises Base Soberanía, Sovereignty, on the black shore of Greenwich Island, the second Chilean station in Antarctica. Serrano walks among the huts and the ice in a light that never wholly dies, keeping his despatches while his mind runs beneath the glacier. Here Chile plants her flag at the bottom of the world; here Serrano begins to read the white continent as a text of Atlantis and Hyperborea, a great white island fallen from the sky, and to ask whether the defeated of the war have withdrawn, as the legend says, into warm oases hidden under the eternal ice.

stops.name: Deception Island, the narrow entrance of the caldera
stops.campa: The ship threads the Neptune's Bellows, the narrow gap in the drowned volcano of Deception Island, into the black flooded caldera where the beaches steam and the ice draws back from waters warmed by the fire below. Here is the very image of his myth made land: a warm oasis ringed by ice, a hidden harbour entered by a single narrow mouth. On the voyage he is reading Jung on the ego and the unconscious, and the whole white continent turns to a country of archetypes. He will write of penetrating again, in the spirit, through the narrow entrance of Deception Island.

stops.name: The unnamed massif, the mountain that bore his name
stops.campa: In gratitude for his voyage the expedition names a mountain of the white land for him, so that for a season a peak at the bottom of the world carries the name Serrano, though later the name is taken away and given to another. It is, for the mythographer, a perfect emblem: a mountain of ice bearing his name and then unnamed, a summit at the pole, present and erased at once. He has planted himself, if only for a moment, upon the very axis of the earth that his cosmos will make its centre.

stops.name: The South Pole, the entrance to the Inner Earth (Symmes's hollow)
stops.campa: In Serrano's cosmos the pole is a door. Below the axis, where Symmes long ago set the mouth of his hollow world, lies the entrance to the Inner Earth: the warm oasis at the heart of the ice, the refuge of the Hyperboreans and of the Führer who, he insists, did not die but withdrew. The two openings of the planet answer each other, north and south; the poles are not places but thresholds. He gazes across the ice-cap toward that hidden mouth. His whole later mythology, Nos, the resurrection, the return, will hang upon this conviction born on the ice.
